# What this vignette covers

A kernel-weighted mean tells you how much of a cover type surrounds a survey
point. It says nothing about how that cover is arranged, or how many cover
types share the neighborhood. Landscape metrics describe those properties.
`landscape_var()` computes 25 of them from a categorical raster, meaning a
raster whose cell values are integer class codes, within a circular buffer
around each survey point. Each metric then enters your model as a covariate.

This vignette shows what each family of metrics measures, which scales you can
fix and which you can estimate, and how to read a fitted coefficient in the
metric's own units. You will add two metrics to the count model from
`vignette("v01-quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")`, then estimate the buffer
radius of a metric from counts simulated with a known answer. Read the Quick
Start first. `vignette("v05-surface-metrics", package = "multiScaleR")`
follows the same steps for continuous rasters.

# Know what each metric family measures

Every metric summarizes the cells inside a circle around a survey point. The
circle has a hard edge, so each cell inside it counts equally and each cell
outside it counts for nothing. The table gives the ecological meaning and the
units of each family. Units assume a raster whose map units are meters.

| Family | Metrics | What it measures | Units |
|:-------|:--------|:-----------------|:------|
| Composition | `shdi`, `shei` (Shannon diversity and evenness), `sidi`, `siei` (Simpson diversity and evenness), `msidi`, `msiei` (modified Simpson diversity and evenness), `pr`, `prd`, `rpr` (patch richness, its density, and its relative form), `ta` (total area) | How many cover types the neighborhood holds and how evenly they share it | `shdi` and `msidi` in log units. Evenness indices and `sidi` run from 0 to 1. `pr` is a count of classes, `prd` is classes per 100 ha, `rpr` is a percentage, and `ta` is in hectares |
| Edge | `ed` (edge density), `te` (total edge), `lsi` (landscape shape index) | How much boundary separates different cover types, which rises as cover breaks into smaller pieces | `ed` in meters of edge per hectare, `te` in meters, `lsi` as a unitless ratio |
| Aggregation | `ai` (aggregation index), `pladj` (proportion of like adjacencies), `contag` (contagion), `iji` (interspersion and juxtaposition) | Whether cells of one cover type sit next to each other or are mixed among other types | Percentages |
| Information theory | `ent` (marginal entropy), `joinent` (joint entropy), `condent` (conditional entropy), `mutinf` (mutual information), `relmutinf` (relative mutual information) | How complex the pattern is, split into what is present and how predictable a neighboring cell is | Log units, except `relmutinf`, which runs from 0 to 1 |
| Class level | `pland` (percentage of landscape), `ca` (class area), `clumpy` (clumpiness index) | How much of the neighborhood one focal cover type fills, and how clumped that type is | `pland` as a percentage, `ca` in hectares, `clumpy` from -1 (dispersed) through 0 (random) to 1 (clumped) |

Four details apply across the table.

- **Log units.** `shdi` and the four entropy metrics use the natural logarithm
  by default, which gives nats. Set `base = 2` in `landscape_var()` to report
  them in bits.
- **Class-level metrics need a focal class.** Supply it with `class`, an
  integer that matches one of the raster's class codes. Asking for `pland`,
  `ca`, or `clumpy` without `class` is an error, and so is supplying `class`
  to any other metric. Where the focal class is absent from a buffer, `pland`
  and `ca` return 0 and `clumpy` returns `NA`.
- **Some metrics need several classes.** `contag` needs at least two classes
  in a buffer and `iji` needs at least three. With fewer, they return `NA`.
- **`rpr` needs a maximum.** Set `classes_max` to the number of cover types
  that could occur.

The information-theory metrics treat the table of adjacent class pairs as a
probability distribution, following Nowosad and Stepinski (2019). The help page
`?msr_vars` defines every metric.

# Decide which scales to fix and which to estimate

The scale of a covariate is the distance over which the landscape is
summarized. For a landscape metric that distance is the buffer radius. The
`radius` argument decides whether you fix it or estimate it, and the choice is
open for all 25 metrics.

| How you write the covariate | What sets the scale | What `multiScale_optim()` reports |
|:----------------------------|:--------------------|:----------------------------------|
| `landscape_var("cover", metric = "ed", radius = 500)` | You do. The metric is computed once within 500 map units | No scale. The metric is an ordinary covariate |
| `landscape_var("cover", metric = "ed")` | The data. The radius is estimated with the model | The radius, without a standard error. Profile-likelihood limits come from `summary(fit, profile = TRUE)` |
| `kernel_var("cover")` | The data. The kernel width, sigma, is estimated with the model | Sigma with a standard error and confidence interval |

A landscape metric has no kernel-weighted form. Its estimated scale is always
a hard radius, and the likelihood changes in small steps as cells enter the
buffer. That is why no standard error is reported for it. Estimating a radius
uses the default `backend = "refit"` of `multiScale_optim()`.

> **What this means for your study.** Fix the radius when you have a biological
> reason for a distance, such as a home-range radius. Estimate it when the
> scale is itself the question, and report the profile-likelihood limits with
> it.

# Work through an example

## Load the data

The example uses the counts, survey points, and raster from the Quick Start.
The counts were simulated to respond to the kernel-weighted mean of `land1`
(sigma of 250 m, effect of -0.5) and of `land2` (sigma of 500 m, effect of
0.7). No landscape metric entered the simulation.

```{r load-data}
data("landscape_counts")   # data frame: counts and one site-level covariate
dat <- landscape_counts

data("surv_pts")           # survey locations (an sf object from the package)
pts <- vect(surv_pts)      # convert to a terra SpatVector

# Three landscape layers on one grid, in meters
land_rast <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                              package = "multiScaleR"))
```

`land1` is a binary habitat layer, which already counts as a categorical
raster. To have a layer with more than two cover types, cut the continuous
`land3` layer into three classes. In your own analysis this would be a mapped
land-cover product.

```{r build-landcover}
# Class 1 below 0.45, class 2 from 0.45 to 0.55, class 3 above 0.55
landcover <- classify(
  land_rast$land3,
  rcl = matrix(c(-Inf, 0.45, 1,
                 0.45, 0.55, 2,
                 0.55,  Inf, 3),
               ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
)
names(landcover) <- "landcover"

# The source layers for this example, on one grid
metric_rasters <- c(land_rast$land1, land_rast$land2, landcover)
```

```{r plot-inputs, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "***The binary habitat layer and the three-class land-cover layer.***"}
plot(metric_rasters[[c("land1", "landcover")]])
```

## Define the covariates

`msr_vars()` names each model covariate and says how to derive it from a
source layer. One source layer can supply several covariates. Here `land1`
supplies both a kernel-weighted proportion of habitat and an edge density.

```{r define-vars}
scale_vars <- msr_vars(
  land1_prop     = kernel_var("land1"),     # proportion of habitat, sigma estimated
  land2_mean     = kernel_var("land2"),     # mean of land2, sigma estimated
  land1_ed_500   = landscape_var("land1", metric = "ed",
                                 radius = 500),   # edge density within 500 m
  cover_shdi_500 = landscape_var("landcover", metric = "shdi",
                                 radius = 500)    # Shannon diversity within 500 m
)

scale_vars[, c("covariate", "source", "type", "metric", "radius", "optimize")]
```

**How to read the output:** Each row is one model covariate. `source` is the
raster layer it comes from. `optimize` is `TRUE` for the two kernel covariates,
whose sigma will be estimated, and `FALSE` for the two metrics, whose radius is
fixed at 500 m.

## Compute the metrics at the survey points

Pass the specification to `kernel_prep()` through `scale_vars`. It extracts the
cells within `max_D` of each point and computes every covariate.

```{r kernel-prep}
kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(
  pts          = pts,              # survey locations
  raster_stack = metric_rasters,   # source layers named in scale_vars
  max_D        = 1700,             # largest distance (m) considered
  kernel       = "gaussian",       # kernel for the two kernel covariates
  scale_vars   = scale_vars,
  verbose      = FALSE
)

# Mean and standard deviation of each covariate, in its own units
round(sapply(kernel_inputs$scl_params, function(x) x), 3)
```

**How to read the output:** `kernel_inputs$kernel_dat` holds the covariates
after centering and scaling, which is what the model uses. `scl_params` keeps
the mean and standard deviation that were removed, in the units of each
metric. Edge density of `land1` averages
`r round(kernel_inputs$scl_params$mean["land1_ed_500"])` m of edge per hectare
across the survey points, with a standard deviation of
`r round(kernel_inputs$scl_params$sd["land1_ed_500"])` m/ha. Shannon diversity
averages `r round(kernel_inputs$scl_params$mean["cover_shdi_500"], 2)` with a
standard deviation of
`r round(kernel_inputs$scl_params$sd["cover_shdi_500"], 2)`. For three classes
its largest possible value is `log(3)`, about 1.10. The rows for
the two kernel covariates are provisional, because they were computed at a
starting sigma.

`kernel_prep()` stops with an error when a metric takes the same value at
every survey point, because a constant cannot be scaled or used as a
covariate. Patch richness within 500 m does that here, since every buffer
holds all three classes.

## Fit the model

Fit the starting model with the derived covariates, then let
`multiScale_optim()` estimate the two kernel scales. The two metrics were
computed once and stay as they are.

```{r fit-model}
df <- data.frame(dat, kernel_inputs$kernel_dat)

# Starting model: formula and family carry through to the optimizer
mod <- glm(counts ~ site + land1_prop + land2_mean +
             land1_ed_500 + cover_shdi_500,
           family = poisson(),
           data   = df)

# Estimate sigma for land1_prop and land2_mean
opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod    = mod,
                        kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs,
                        verbose       = FALSE)
```

## Read the estimated scale

```{r summary}
summary(opt)
```

```{r read-scale, include = FALSE}
est    <- summary(opt)$opt_scale     # sigma, SE, and 95% interval (m)
dist90 <- kernel_dist(opt)           # radius holding 90% of kernel weight (m)
```

**How to read the `summary()` output:** The scale tables list only the two
kernel covariates. Sigma for `land1_prop` is `r round(est["land1_prop", "Mean"])`
m, with a 95% interval of `r round(est["land1_prop", "2.5%"])` to
`r round(est["land1_prop", "97.5%"])` m that contains the true 250 m. Sigma for
`land2_mean` is `r round(est["land2_mean", "Mean"])` m, against a true 500 m.
The distance table converts each sigma to the radius that holds 90% of the
kernel weight, which is `r round(dist90["land1_prop", "Mean"])` m for
`land1_prop` and `r round(dist90["land2_mean", "Mean"])` m for `land2_mean`.
Edge density and Shannon diversity are absent from the scale tables because
you set their radius. They appear only in the regression table, as ordinary
covariates measured within 500 m.

## Interpret a coefficient in the metric's units

The regression coefficients are on the log scale, because the model is Poisson
with a log link. Each one describes a change of one standard deviation,
because the covariates were standardized. Two steps turn a coefficient into a
statement about the metric. Divide by the metric's standard deviation to get
the effect of one unit, then exponentiate to get a multiplicative change in
the expected count.

```{r coef-units}
beta <- coef(opt$opt_mod)              # log scale, per one standard deviation
ci   <- confint.default(opt$opt_mod)   # Wald 95% limits, log scale
sds  <- opt$scl_params$sd              # one standard deviation, in metric units

# A step that is easy to picture, in the units of each metric
step <- c(land1_ed_500   = 10,         # 10 m more edge per hectare
          cover_shdi_500 = 0.1)        # 0.1 more Shannon diversity
m <- names(step)

effect <- data.frame(
  Covariate  = m,
  SD         = sds[m],
  Step       = step,
  Multiplier = exp(beta[m]  * step / sds[m]),   # change in expected count
  Lower      = exp(ci[m, 1] * step / sds[m]),
  Upper      = exp(ci[m, 2] * step / sds[m])
)
knitr::kable(effect, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

**How to read the table:** `Multiplier` is the factor by which the expected
count changes when the metric rises by `Step`, with the other covariates held
constant. An increase of 10 m/ha in edge density within 500 m multiplies the
expected count by `r sprintf("%.2f", effect$Multiplier[1])`, with a 95%
interval of `r sprintf("%.2f", effect$Lower[1])` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", effect$Upper[1])`. An increase of 0.1 in Shannon diversity
multiplies it by `r sprintf("%.2f", effect$Multiplier[2])`
(`r sprintf("%.2f", effect$Lower[2])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", effect$Upper[2])`). Both
intervals include 1, which means no change. That is the right answer here,
because neither metric was used to simulate the counts. The intervals treat
the estimated sigma values as known, as explained in
`vignette("v09-estimates-and-intervals", package = "multiScaleR")`.

# Estimate the scale of a metric

The running example has no metric effect to recover, so this section simulates
one. The counts below respond to edge density of `land1` within 400 m, with an
effect of 0.5 on the log scale for each standard deviation of edge density.

```{r sim-truth}
# Edge density within 400 m, the scale used to simulate the counts
truth_inputs <- kernel_prep(
  pts          = pts,
  raster_stack = land_rast["land1"],
  max_D        = 1200,
  scale_vars   = msr_vars(ed_400 = landscape_var("land1", metric = "ed",
                                                 radius = 400)),
  verbose      = FALSE
)

set.seed(1)
# kernel_dat is standardized, so 0.5 is the effect of one standard deviation
sim_counts <- rpois(100, exp(0.5 + 0.5 * truth_inputs$kernel_dat$ed_400))
```

To estimate the radius, leave `radius` out of `landscape_var()`. Everything
else is the usual workflow.

```{r sim-fit}
# No radius: the buffer radius becomes a parameter of the model
free_vars <- msr_vars(land1_ed = landscape_var("land1", metric = "ed"))

free_inputs <- kernel_prep(
  pts          = pts,
  raster_stack = land_rast["land1"],
  max_D        = 1200,             # the radius is searched up to this distance
  scale_vars   = free_vars,
  verbose      = FALSE
)

sim_df  <- data.frame(counts = sim_counts, free_inputs$kernel_dat)
sim_mod <- glm(counts ~ land1_ed, family = poisson(), data = sim_df)

sim_opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod    = sim_mod,
                            kernel_inputs = free_inputs,
                            verbose       = FALSE)

# Radius with profile-likelihood limits, in meters
sim_scale <- summary(sim_opt, profile = TRUE)$opt_scale
round(sim_scale, 1)
```

**How to read the output:** `Mean` is the estimated buffer radius,
`r round(sim_scale["land1_ed", "Mean"])` m, against the 400 m used to simulate
the counts. `SE` is `NA` because the likelihood changes in steps along a hard
radius, so the usual standard error is not computed. The limits come from the
profile likelihood and run from
`r round(sim_scale["land1_ed", "2.5%"])` to
`r round(sim_scale["land1_ed", "97.5%"])` m. A radius is already a distance, so
it needs no conversion to an effective distance.

```{r sim-profile, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "***AICc across candidate radii for edge density. The dashed line marks the estimate.***"}
# Refit the model at 15 candidate radii
plot(profile_sigma(sim_opt, n_pts = 15, verbose = FALSE))
```

**How to read this plot:** Lower AICc means better support. The horizontal
axis is labeled sigma, which for a landscape metric is the buffer radius in
meters. A single deep trough near the dashed line means the data identify the
radius. A hard-radius profile can also show small bumps, because the metric
changes each time a cell enters the buffer. Judge the profile by its overall
shape.

Interpret the coefficient as before. The standard deviation now belongs to
edge density at the estimated radius.

```{r sim-coef}
sim_beta <- coef(sim_opt$opt_mod)["land1_ed"]             # per standard deviation
sim_ci   <- confint.default(sim_opt$opt_mod)["land1_ed", ]
sim_sd   <- sim_opt$scl_params$sd["land1_ed"]             # m/ha at the fitted radius

# Change in expected count for 10 m more edge per hectare
sim_effect <- exp(c(Estimate = unname(sim_beta), Lower = sim_ci[[1]],
                    Upper = sim_ci[[2]]) * 10 / sim_sd)
round(sim_effect, 3)

# The value used in the simulation, on the same footing
round(exp(0.5 * 10 / truth_inputs$scl_params$sd["ed_400"]), 3)
```

**How to read the output:** Within the estimated radius, each additional 10 m
of edge per hectare multiplies the expected count by
`r sprintf("%.2f", sim_effect["Estimate"])`, an increase of
`r round(100 * (sim_effect["Estimate"] - 1))`%. The 95% interval runs from
`r sprintf("%.2f", sim_effect["Lower"])` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", sim_effect["Upper"])` and
contains the simulated value on the last line.

```{r sim-marginal, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "***Expected count across the observed range of edge density at the estimated radius.***"}
plot_marginal_effects(sim_opt)
```

**How to read this plot:** The horizontal axis is edge density in m/ha, not
the standardized covariate, so you can read expected counts directly against
the metric. The shaded band is a 95% confidence band for the expected count
that treats the estimated radius as known.

> **What this means for your study.** Changing the radius of a landscape metric
> changes the quantity, not only its smoothness. Edge density within 200 m and
> within 900 m are different covariates with different ranges, so compare
> coefficients only after converting each to the metric's units at its own
> radius.

Estimating a radius costs more than estimating a kernel sigma, because the
metric is recomputed for every survey point at each candidate radius. Settle
the model structure with fixed radii first. Before you estimate a radius for
`iji`, `siei`, or `msiei`, compute the metric at a few fixed radii and confirm
that it varies among survey points. These metrics can be `NA` or nearly
constant when buffers hold too few classes or too few boundaries between
classes.

## Search a list of radii

The optimizer above searches the radius continuously. You can instead name the
radii to compare, such as distances that match the home-range sizes of your
species, and refit the model at each one. Pass them to `radius_grid` with the
default `refit` backend. This search is experimental.

```{r radius-grid}
# Refit the model at nine radii from 200 to 1,000 m
grid_fit <- multiScale_optim(sim_mod, free_inputs, backend = "refit",
                             radius_grid = seq(200, 1000, by = 100),
                             verbose = FALSE)
radii <- diagnostics(grid_fit)$radius_profile
radii[, c("radius", "log_likelihood", "status", "selected")]
```

**How to read the output:** Each row is one candidate radius and the
log-likelihood of the model refitted there. Higher is better. `selected` marks
the best row, `r radii$radius[radii$selected]` m, and `status` would name the
reason if a refit failed. The neighboring radii of 300 and 500 m fit worse by
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(radii$log_likelihood) - radii$log_likelihood[radii$radius == 300])`
and
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(radii$log_likelihood) - radii$log_likelihood[radii$radius == 500])`
log-likelihood units, so the data clearly favor 400 m, the radius used to
simulate the counts. A flat run of rows means the data barely distinguish
those radii. A best row at either end of the list means the search should
extend further. The grid gives no standard error or interval for the radius.

For several metrics with estimated radii, pass a named list with one vector
per covariate, for example
`radius_grid = list(diversity = c(250, 500, 750), edge = c(300, 500, 900))`.
Every combination is fitted, nine in that case, and any kernel sigma in the
same model is re-estimated at each. The best radius for one metric can depend
on the radius of the other, which is why they are searched together. The same
argument works for a step-selection model, and
`vignette("v08-cross-validation", package = "multiScaleR")` shows how to repeat
the search inside cross-validation folds.

# Map the metrics

## Map the covariates of a fitted model

`kernel_scale.raster()` applies each covariate definition to the whole raster.
Given a fitted model, it uses the estimated sigma for kernel covariates and
the stated radius for fixed-radius metrics.

```{r project, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "***The covariates of the fitted model, in their own units.***"}
projected <- kernel_scale.raster(raster_stack = metric_rasters,
                                 multiScaleR  = opt,       # the fitted object
                                 verbose      = FALSE)
names(projected)

plot(projected[[1:4]])
```

**How to read these plots:** Each layer carries the name of a model covariate
and is in that covariate's units. `land1_prop` is a proportion of habitat,
`land1_ed_500` is meters of edge per hectare, and `cover_shdi_500` is Shannon
diversity. Diversity is highest along the band where the three cover classes
meet and lowest inside the large blocks of a single class. The fifth layer,
`site`, is a constant zero. `site` was measured at the survey points and has
no raster, so the function adds a placeholder to let the stack go straight to
`terra::predict()`.

To predict from the model, add `scale_center = TRUE` so the layers are
standardized as the model's covariates were, and `clamp = TRUE` to stay inside
the fitted range. `vignette("v03-map-predictions", package = "multiScaleR")`
covers prediction maps.

## Map a metric without a model

You do not need a fitted model to map a metric. Pass a specification in which
every covariate has a fixed radius.

```{r standalone-multiscale, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3, fig.cap = "***Edge density of land1 (m/ha) at three radii.***"}
ed_multi <- kernel_scale.raster(
  raster_stack = metric_rasters["land1"],
  scale_vars   = msr_vars(
    ed_200 = landscape_var("land1", metric = "ed", radius = 200),
    ed_500 = landscape_var("land1", metric = "ed", radius = 500),
    ed_900 = landscape_var("land1", metric = "ed", radius = 900)
  ),
  verbose = FALSE
)

# Range of each surface, in m of edge per hectare
round(t(global(ed_multi, c("min", "max"), na.rm = TRUE)))

plot(ed_multi, nc = 3, mar = c(2, 2, 2, 5))   # room for each legend
```

**How to read these plots:** The same metric looks different at each radius. At
200 m the surface is patchy, with the lowest minimum and the highest maximum
of the three. At 900 m each buffer averages over more of the landscape, so the
surface is smoother and its range is narrower. This is the reason an estimated radius matters.

## Separate composition from configuration

Composition is what the neighborhood contains. Configuration is how those
contents are arranged. The information-theory metrics describe both for the
same buffer.

```{r info-theory-surfaces, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3, fig.cap = "***Marginal entropy, mutual information, and relative mutual information of the land-cover layer within 500 m.***"}
info_surfaces <- kernel_scale.raster(
  raster_stack = metric_rasters["landcover"],
  scale_vars   = msr_vars(
    H_x   = landscape_var("landcover", metric = "ent",
                          radius = 500, base = 2),      # bits
    MI    = landscape_var("landcover", metric = "mutinf",
                          radius = 500, base = 2),      # bits
    relMI = landscape_var("landcover", metric = "relmutinf",
                          radius = 500)                 # 0 to 1
  ),
  verbose = FALSE
)

plot(info_surfaces, nc = 3, mar = c(2, 2, 2, 5))   # room for each legend
```

**How to read these plots:** Marginal entropy (`H_x`, in bits because
`base = 2`) describes composition. It is high where a buffer holds the three
classes in similar amounts and low where one class dominates. With three
classes it cannot exceed `log2(3)`, about 1.58 bits. Mutual information (`MI`)
measures how much a cell's class tells you about its neighbor's class. It
rises where the classes form predictable arrangements, and its size also
depends on marginal entropy. Relative mutual information (`relMI`) divides
mutual information by marginal entropy, which puts it on a 0 to 1 scale that
you can compare between neighborhoods of different composition.

## Describe one cover type

The class-level metrics answer the same two questions for a single class.

```{r clumpy-surface, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "***Percentage cover and clumpiness of land-cover class 2 within 500 m.***"}
class2_surfaces <- kernel_scale.raster(
  raster_stack = metric_rasters["landcover"],
  scale_vars   = msr_vars(
    pland2  = landscape_var("landcover", metric = "pland",
                            radius = 500, class = 2),   # percent of the buffer
    clumpy2 = landscape_var("landcover", metric = "clumpy",
                            radius = 500, class = 2)    # -1 to 1
  ),
  verbose = FALSE
)

plot(class2_surfaces)
```

**How to read these plots:** `pland2` is the percentage of each 500 m buffer
occupied by class 2. `clumpy2` is positive everywhere on this map, which means
class 2 is more aggregated than a random arrangement of the same amount of
cover would be. Because `clumpy` corrects for how much of the class is
present, the two maps need not agree.

# Check these before you fit

- **Class codes.** `landscape_var()` requires integer class codes. Classify a
  continuous raster first, or use
  `vignette("v05-surface-metrics", package = "multiScaleR")` for metrics
  designed for continuous values.
- **Number of classes.** The aggregation and information-theory metrics accept
  a limited number of classes. The limit is 200 for `ai`, `pladj`, and
  `clumpy`, and 50 for `contag`, `iji`, and the information-theory family.
- **Variation among points.** A metric that barely varies among survey points
  cannot explain the response. Check `kernel_inputs$scl_params$sd` before
  fitting.
- **Units.** Edge and area metrics are in meters and hectares only when the
  raster's map units are meters.
- **Method support.** `vignette("v07-fitting-methods", package = "multiScaleR")`
  lists which fitting methods accept landscape metrics.

# Quick reference

```{r quick-reference, eval = FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
library(terra)

# 1. Load the data and build a categorical layer
data("landscape_counts"); data("surv_pts")
dat       <- landscape_counts
pts       <- vect(surv_pts)
land_rast <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                              package = "multiScaleR"))
landcover <- classify(land_rast$land3,
                      rcl = matrix(c(-Inf, 0.45, 1,
                                     0.45, 0.55, 2,
                                     0.55,  Inf, 3), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE))
names(landcover) <- "landcover"
metric_rasters <- c(land_rast$land1, land_rast$land2, landcover)

# 2. Define the covariates: two kernel means and two fixed-radius metrics
scale_vars <- msr_vars(
  land1_prop     = kernel_var("land1"),
  land2_mean     = kernel_var("land2"),
  land1_ed_500   = landscape_var("land1", metric = "ed", radius = 500),
  cover_shdi_500 = landscape_var("landcover", metric = "shdi", radius = 500)
)

# 3. Compute the covariates at the survey points
kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = metric_rasters,
                             max_D = 1700, kernel = "gaussian",
                             scale_vars = scale_vars, verbose = FALSE)
kernel_inputs$scl_params            # mean and SD of each metric, in its units

# 4. Fit the model and estimate the kernel scales
df  <- data.frame(dat, kernel_inputs$kernel_dat)
mod <- glm(counts ~ site + land1_prop + land2_mean +
             land1_ed_500 + cover_shdi_500,
           family = poisson(), data = df)
opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod = mod, kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs,
                        verbose = FALSE)
summary(opt)                        # sigma, effective distance, regression table

# 5. Read a metric coefficient in the metric's units
beta <- coef(opt$opt_mod)
sds  <- opt$scl_params$sd
exp(beta["land1_ed_500"] * 10 / sds["land1_ed_500"])   # per 10 m/ha of edge

# 6. Estimate the radius of a metric: leave radius out
set.seed(1)
truth_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast["land1"],
                            max_D = 1200, verbose = FALSE,
                            scale_vars = msr_vars(
                              ed_400 = landscape_var("land1", metric = "ed",
                                                     radius = 400)))
sim_counts  <- rpois(100, exp(0.5 + 0.5 * truth_inputs$kernel_dat$ed_400))
free_vars   <- msr_vars(land1_ed = landscape_var("land1", metric = "ed"))
free_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast["land1"],
                           max_D = 1200, scale_vars = free_vars,
                           verbose = FALSE)
sim_df  <- data.frame(counts = sim_counts, free_inputs$kernel_dat)
sim_mod <- glm(counts ~ land1_ed, family = poisson(), data = sim_df)
sim_opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod = sim_mod, kernel_inputs = free_inputs,
                            verbose = FALSE)
summary(sim_opt, profile = TRUE)$opt_scale     # radius with profile limits
plot(profile_sigma(sim_opt, n_pts = 15, verbose = FALSE))   # AICc by radius
grid_fit <- multiScale_optim(sim_mod, free_inputs, backend = "refit",
                             radius_grid = seq(200, 1000, by = 100))
diagnostics(grid_fit)$radius_profile        # log-likelihood at each listed radius
plot_marginal_effects(sim_opt)                 # expected count against m/ha

# 7. Map the covariates of a fitted model, or a metric on its own
projected <- kernel_scale.raster(raster_stack = metric_rasters,
                                 multiScaleR = opt, verbose = FALSE)
ed_multi  <- kernel_scale.raster(
  raster_stack = metric_rasters["land1"],
  scale_vars   = msr_vars(
    ed_200 = landscape_var("land1", metric = "ed", radius = 200),
    ed_500 = landscape_var("land1", metric = "ed", radius = 500),
    ed_900 = landscape_var("land1", metric = "ed", radius = 900)),
  verbose = FALSE)
```

## Summary of key functions

| Function | Purpose |
|:---------|:--------|
| `msr_vars()` | Collect named covariate definitions into one specification |
| `kernel_var()` | Define a kernel-weighted mean whose sigma is estimated |
| `landscape_var()` | Define a landscape metric from a categorical raster, with a fixed or estimated radius |
| `kernel_prep()` | Compute the covariates at the survey points and store their means and standard deviations |
| `multiScale_optim()` | Estimate every free sigma and radius together with the regression coefficients |
| `summary()` | Report scales and the regression table. `profile = TRUE` adds profile-likelihood limits |
| `profile_sigma()` | Show how well the data identify each scale |
| `diagnostics()` | With `radius_grid`, the log-likelihood at every listed radius |
| `plot_marginal_effects()` | Draw the expected response against each covariate in its own units |
| `kernel_scale.raster()` | Map covariates, with or without a fitted model |
